transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, doctor. Well, what brought me in is that I've been having some trouble with how much I'm eating at night. 

After my evening class, I sometimes stop for food on the way back. I'll end up eating a full fast-food meal... then I'll grab candy from the vending machine, and when I finally get home, I just keep going with more snacks. It's almost like I'm making up for the whole day in one sitting. I just thought I should probably talk to someone about it.

After these eating episodes at night, do you do anything to try to compensate or make up for what you've eaten, such as making yourself vomit, exercising excessively, or restricting food the next day?

Well, yes. A few times after those late-night eating spells, I've gone into the bathroom and made myself throw up. I just... I was really scared that all that food would start to show on me. I haven't really done the exercise thing you mentioned, but I have made myself sick a couple of times.
How often would you say you've made yourself throw up after these eating episodes—is it happening most of the time after a binge, or just occasionally?

Well, looking back on it, I'd say this has been going on for about the past three months. Usually, there's at least one night each week after my class where I end up overeating like that... and then I make myself throw up afterward. So, I guess it's about once a week.

latest_inference.note: Patient reports recurrent binge eating episodes (at least weekly for 3 months) followed by self-induced vomiting as compensatory behavior. This is consistent with Bulimia Nervosa (F50.81). F50.82 (Binge Eating Disorder) is ruled out because the patient demonstrates regular purging behavior through self-induced vomiting, which is the distinguishing feature of bulimia nervosa.
